title: Mastering Supranuclear Gaze Palsy & The VOR
summary: Supranuclear gaze palsies involve disruption of the supranuclear pathways controlling eye movements, manifesting as loss of voluntary gaze while preserving the Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR). This guide bridges the neuro-anatomical pathways from the frontal eye fields to the brainstem PPRF.

sections.title: Clinical Definition
sections.content: Supranuclear gaze palsy is a clinical condition characterized by the inability to move the eyes in one or more directions of gaze, despite intact cranial nerves (III, IV, VI) and extraocular muscles. It is defined by the integrity of the VOR (doll's head maneuver), which confirms the lesion is superior to the ocular motor nuclei in the brainstem.

sections.title: Epidemiology & Etiology
content: PSP (Progressive Supranuclear Palsy): Most common cause, prevalence ~5/100,000

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Sequence
content: Step 2: Smooth pursuit and Saccadic velocity testing.
Step 3: MRI Brain (High resolution T1/T2, focus on midbrain/pons).
Step 4: Lumbar puncture if neuro-infectious/inflammatory suspected.
Step 5: Genetic testing (MAPT gene for PSP).

content.explanation: S: Supranuclear gaze palsy; T: Tall (often), E: Early falls; E: Extension (posture); L: Limb rigidity; E: Emotional lability.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Vertical gaze palsy often precedes horizontal involvement in PSP.
Square wave jerks are classic findings in supranuclear palsy.
Hummingbird sign (MRI midbrain atrophy) is diagnostic for PSP.

sections.title: Recent Advances
sections.content: Recent research focuses on Tau-pathology mitigation. Landmark studies (e.g., PASSPORT trial) highlight the use of monoclonal antibodies targeting extracellular Tau protein. Digital eye-tracking metrics are now being used as biomarkers for disease progression in clinical trials.
